articles.title: A woman found a dingo puppy in her backyard after it apparently fell from an eagle's claws; two years later, he returned to the sanctuary that raised him
articles.summary: A woman who found a dingo puppy in her backyard, apparently dropped from an eagle’s claws, has been reunited with the animal two years on.
articles.body: A woman who found a dingo puppy in her backyard, apparently dropped from an eagle’s claws, has been reunited with the animal two years on. The puppy, named Wandi, is a rare Alpine Dingo. Jane Guiney found him in north-east Victoria, and DNA testing later confirmed he was a purebred. He was raised at the Dingo Discovery Sanctuary and Research Centre, and he came back to the area where he was found with his partner, Hermione, and two of their puppies. The reunion also took in a visit to a local primary school, whose students had followed Wandi’s remarkable journey.What happened to the dingo puppy two years after his backyard discoveryJane Guiney found Wandi in her backyard in north-east Victoria. According to ABC News, she heard the puppy whining in the yard after he had apparently fallen from an eagle’s claws. He is believed to have been taken from his mother by the eagle when he was between eight and 10 weeks old.Guiney picked the young animal up and looked after him in the early days. DNA testing later confirmed that Wandi was a purebred Alpine Dingo, a rare type of dingo. His discovery drew considerable attention because it offered evidence that pure dingoes were still present in Victoria.How did Wandi find a partner and start a family at the dingo sanctuaryAfter he was found, Wandi was taken to the Dingo Discovery Sanctuary and Research Centre, where he spent the next few years. The sanctuary became his home, and there he met Hermione, who became his partner. The pair had their first litter of puppies in 2021, and the sanctuary kept two of their offspring.Sanctuary supervisor Kevin Newman, who also became Wandi’s manager, called the animal a valuable ambassador for the species. Speaking to ABC News, Newman said: “Even we as a sanctuary had that thought too, until Wandi literally fell from the sky and proved everyone wrong.” He was referring to the belief, once held by some scientists, that no pure dingoes remained in Victoria.How did Jane Guiney react when she reunited with Wandi after two yearsTwo years after he was found, Wandi went back to the area where Guiney had discovered him. The reunion was an emotional one for her, especially as she had cared for him straight after he arrived. Speaking about seeing him again, Guiney told ABC News: “It was an amazing feeling, just looking at the mountains and knowing that this is his home.”She also believed that Wandi recognised her when they met. Describing his behaviour, she said: “The way he came up to me and was getting protection from my son Ed, who was with me when I found him. I’m hoping [he remembered me] anyway.”Wandiligong Primary School made the reunion possible. Its students had been writing letters to Wandi after hearing about his unusual story and forming a connection with the sanctuary. Wandi visited the school with Hermione and their two puppies, Harriet and Jirrikit. The visit gave the students a chance to see the animals and learn more about dingoes.Why are dingoes in Victoria facing conservation challengesWandi’s discovery also drew attention to the conservation challenges facing dingoes in Victoria. Newman told ABC News that the species was threatened in the state and needed greater protection. He estimated that between 600 and 800 dingoes remained in the wild in Victoria, though he acknowledged there was not enough data to give an exact population figure.He also pointed to the legal restrictions affecting the animals. Dingoes are classed as a threatened protected species in Victoria, but an order in council makes an exception for those found on private property or within three kilometres of it. Newman said the sanctuary wanted this arrangement changed, explaining: “They are a threatened protected species in Victoria ... they need our help and they need our protection.”How does 1080 poison threaten dingoes in the wildNewman raised another concern: the use of meat baits containing 1080 poison. These baits are used across Australia to protect agricultural production and native flora and fauna from the effects of pest animals. Dingoes can also fall victim to the poison, which affects their numbers in the wild.Newman referred to a Victorian ecosystem decline inquiry and its recommendations on how dingoes should be managed in future. He told ABC News that the recommendations included phasing out the use of 1080 poison and looking into the possibility of reintroducing dingoes into the wild.Wandi’s story has also raised public interest in the species. According to Newman, the misconception that dingoes are simply wild dogs has fed misunderstandings about their conservation status. Since Wandi was found, four dingo puppies have turned up around the Alpine area, bringing further attention to the species in the region.His return to the place where he was first found brought him back to the woman who first cared for him and to the community that had followed his journey. By then, Wandi had become an ambassador for dingoes through his work at the sanctuary and the attention his discovery brought to the species.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: Bronze gravesite vase thefts in Burnaby, British Columbia, prompted a police investigation after several hundred of the memorial fixtures were believed to have been taken from local cemeteries over a period of months. The vases sat directly on grave markers, giving grieving visitors somewhere to leave flowers for those they had lost. Officers said the combined loss could run to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Police stressed, however, that the financial cost was not the real measure of the harm.Corporal Mike Kalanj of the Burnaby detachment said, “The monetary value, while high, pales in comparison to the sentimental value these items hold for grieving families.”Kalanj described the thefts in blunt terms. “Stealing from a final resting place is a disgusting act that causes significant emotional distress to those already dealing with loss,” he said. articles.title: A Washington couple divorced in 2021, remarried in 2022 and split again eight months later; a November 3 court upheld a property deal that left the wife without bank and stock assets awarded in their first divorce
articles.summary: A divorce settlement can settle who owns an asset on paper, but what happens when a couple gets back together and later separates again?
articles.body: A divorce settlement can settle who owns an asset on paper, but what happens when a couple gets back together and later separates again? A Washington woman faced this situation after remarrying her former husband and separating again approximately eight months later. Although their first divorce settlement had awarded her half of several bank accounts and stock assets, most remained in her former husband's name. When they divorced again, a new property agreement and arbitration decision left her without those assets.In an unpublished opinion dated November 3, 2026, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division II, upheld the lower court's decision in In the Matter of the Marriage of William Gibbs and Joy Ann Gibbs, case number 60590-2-II. The ruling, available on Justia, affirmed an arbitration award favouring William Gibbs and rejected Joy Gibbs' attempt to challenge the decision through a request for a new trial. The court also awarded William reasonable attorney fees for the appeal.The first divorce divided their propertyWilliam and Joy Gibbs married in 1998 and divorced in 2021. During their first divorce, they reached a mediated settlement that divided their assets into separate property. Under the agreement, Joy received half of several assets, including a BNY Mellon 401(k), joint USAA savings and checking accounts, restricted stock units (RSUs), their ownership interest in Conner's Pretzel and Wine company, and their wine collection. William retained an E-Trade Rollover IRA held in his name. However, although Joy was awarded half of these assets, most remained registered under William's name. She successfully transferred half of the BNY Mellon 401(k) into her own name, but the other assets were not similarly transferred.The couple remarried in November 2022, but their second marriage lasted approximately eight to nine months. During the subsequent divorce proceedings, Joy sought to enforce the original 2021 decree. The superior court partly granted her request, enforcing the earlier division for the period between their first divorce and remarriage. However, it left questions about the assets after their remarriage unresolved, stating that issues involving the tracing and possible mixing of separate property needed further examination.A second agreement changed the arrangementWilliam and Joy subsequently participated in another mediation to resolve their property disputes. Joy did not personally attend, but her attorney and her father, who acted as her power of attorney, represented her. The mediation resulted in a CR 2A agreement, which established how their property would be divided. It stated that the marital home would be divided equally, while each party would retain all other assets and debts held in their respective names.Importantly, the agreement also stated that it superseded the 2021 divorce decree and that all orders under the earlier decree were considered satisfied. It further prohibited either party from starting enforcement proceedings relating to that decree.The agreement required disagreements concerning the preparation of final orders to be resolved through binding arbitration. When William and Joy could not agree on how to implement its terms, the dispute went to an arbitrator.Arbitration awarded the accounts and stock to WilliamThe arbitrator interpreted the second agreement to mean that each party would retain assets held in their respective names, unless they had agreed otherwise. As a result, Joy received the half of the BNY Mellon 401(k) that she had already transferred into her name. However, she did not receive half of the USAA accounts or the restricted stock units awarded to her in the first divorce because those assets remained registered under William's name. The arbitrator awarded the accounts and stock units to William.There were some exceptions. The couple agreed to divide their ownership interests in three companies, including Conner's Pretzel and Wine, equally. Their wine collection was also divided equally because it was not registered under either person's name. Joy challenged the decision and sought reconsideration, but the arbitrator rejected her request. She then approached the superior court, seeking a new trial under a rule that had already been repealed.Court rejected her request for a new trialJoy filed her request under Superior Court Mandatory Arbitration Rules (MAR) 7.1. However, the rules had been repealed in 2019 and replaced by the Superior Court Civil Arbitration Rules. The superior court rejected her request and confirmed the arbitration award. During the hearing, the possibility of filing a motion to vacate the arbitration award was discussed, but Joy's lawyer did not formally submit such a motion or ask the court to treat the existing request as one.On appeal, Joy argued that her request should have been treated as a motion to vacate because she was challenging the arbitrator's failure to recognise her ownership rights under the first divorce decree. She maintained that her half of the USAA accounts and RSUs had already become vested and should not have been taken away through the second agreement.The appeals court disagreed, finding that her original filing was too limited to be interpreted as a proper motion to vacate. It did not explain the legal grounds for setting aside the arbitration award or establish that the arbitrator had exceeded their authority. The court also noted that her lawyer had an opportunity to correct the procedural issue but did not do so.Appeals court upheld the arbitration awardThe Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court's decision and awarded William reasonable attorney fees for the appeal under the second agreement. The court did not decide the underlying question of whether Joy's ownership rights under the first divorce decree had been legally extinguished. Instead, it declined to consider those arguments because they had not been properly raised before the superior court.As a result, the arbitration award remained in place, leaving the USAA accounts and restricted stock units with William.You use AI every day. articles.title: 24-hour deadline starts with detention: SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday ruled that the constitutional mandate of producing an arrestee before a magistrate within 24 hours starts the moment one
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday ruled that the constitutional mandate of producing an arrestee before a magistrate within 24 hours starts the moment one is detained for interrogation and not from the time when formal arrest is made by an investigating agency, since the liberty of a person is curtailed when one is detained.Noting that no artificial distinction should be created between detention and arrest, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar quashed the verdicts of high courts which had held that the 24-hour period starts only after formal arrest and not during antecedent detention necessitated by statutory procedure of seizure. Article 22(2) mandates that every person who is arrested and detained in custody has to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of such arrest."Article 22(2) does not sanction exclusion of the time taken for enquiry and investigation before the arresting authority could effect arrest of the detainee. This is beyond the mandate of Article 22(2) of the Constitution. Article 22(2) does not sanction creation of any buffer zone where the liberty of an individual is curtailed for investigating purposes but not formally shown as arrested. Creation or contemplation of such buffer zone is unconstitutional..." the bench said.As it is common practice for police to record formal arrest much later, sometimes even a day after detaining a person for interrogation, Supreme Court's order would serve as a check on the police and other investigating agencies. The court also noted that its order was meant to eliminate custodial violence, which unfortunately takes place during the time when a person is under detention and not shown as formally arrested, in the process delaying production before the magistrate.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Umar, Sharjeel move SC for bail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Referring to the contradictory orders given by Supreme Court in the matter of bail to the accused on the ground of delay in trial and long
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Referring to the contradictory orders given by Supreme Court in the matter of bail to the accused on the ground of delay in trial and long incarceration for UAPA offences, which have been referred to a larger bench for authoritative pronouncement, former student activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam have moved SC for bail in 2020 Delhi riots cases.The accused submitted that two co-accused, including Tasleem Ahmed, were granted bail by SC on the grou-nd that determination of the issues by the larger bench would take time, and they could not be made to suffer continued incarceration.Seeking parity with the co-accused, Sharjeel Imam, who has already spent six years and nine months in custody, said in his petition, filed through advocate Fauzia Shakil, that two co-accused in the same FIR were released on interim bail by the court on May 22 under a principle which applies to him in greater degree.The accused moved SC after their plea for bail was rejected by the trial court and Delhi High Court on the ground that the apex court had purportedly set a deadline of Jan 5, 2027, for them to file a bail petition.The petition asked "whether the principle recognised by this Court in Tasleem Ahmed v. State order dated 22.05.2026, that an accused cannot be made to suffer continued incarceration merely because an important question of law has arisen for authoritative settlement, can be withheld from the petitioner alone by reference to the role attributed to him, when the question referred to concerns the correctness of the very judgment which declined his bail and relief in Tasleem Ahmed case was granted without any examination of role?"It further argued, "Whether liberty reserved by this Court in a judgment declining bail, to renew the prayer for bail at a defined point, operates as a bar upon the statutory jurisdiction of the Special Court and of the High Court to consider an application for bail founded on supervening circumstances be-fore that point, when the same paragraph of the judgment holds that pre-trial detention cannot be permitted to continue without regard to the progress of the trial and that Article 21 operates as a continuing check against continued incarceration without substantial progress of the trial?"Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Georgia developer planned 97 townhomes, 46 of them within 1,000 feet of a proposed waste facility; a November 2 court upheld the facility's permit because the homes were still unbuilt when the application was submitted
articles.summary: A proposed residential neighbourhood can face uncertainty when an industrial facility is planned nearby, particularly when future homes fall within the
articles.body: A proposed residential neighbourhood can face uncertainty when an industrial facility is planned nearby, particularly when future homes fall within the distance restricted by local zoning rules. A Georgia developer faced this situation after a county approved a permit for a waste processing facility near its planned 97-townhome community. Although 46 of the proposed homes were within 1,000 feet of the proposed waste handling area, construction had not begun when the facility's permit application was submitted.In an opinion dated November 2, 2026, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld the permit approval in Norhaven Partners, LLC et al. v. Bartow County et al., case number A26A1626. The ruling, available on Justia, rejected the developer's challenge to Bartow County's decision to grant a conditional use permit to Justin Rice and Rice Commercial Investments, Inc. The court concluded that the county's zoning restriction applied to constructed residential buildings or structures, rather than undeveloped land designated for future homes.Developer planned 97 townhomes near industrial propertyThe dispute involved two neighbouring properties in Bartow County, Georgia. In January 2023, the county approved conceptual site plans submitted by Norhaven Partners and Peeples Owner LLC for a 97-unit townhome development known as Overlook on Pettit. By October 2023, the plans had received full approval, including a land use disturbance permit.The neighbouring property, located east of the proposed community, was zoned for heavy industrial use and belonged to Justin Rice. It was already being used for activities such as mulch materials processing, wood shredding and rock crushing.On July 2, 2024, Rice applied for a conditional use permit (CUP) to expand operations to include a recovered materials processing and solid waste handling facility for construction and demolition materials. The proposal raised concerns for Norhaven because an overlay of the two development plans showed that 46 of its 97 planned townhomes would fall within 1,000 feet of the proposed waste handling area. The developer argued that the facility would violate the county's zoning restrictions.Zoning ordinance became central to the disputeThe main issue involved Section 9.5.6 of the Bartow County Zoning Ordinance. It prohibited a waste handling area, measured from the chain-link fence boundary, from being located within 1,000 feet of any residential dwelling used at the time of the permit application. Norhaven relied on another provision, Section 3.1, which stated that the terms 'used' or 'occupied' included land or buildings intended, arranged or designed for use or occupancy. It argued that its approved townhome development should receive protection under this provision even though the homes had not been constructed.However, Section 3.2 defined a dwelling as a building or other structure designed, arranged or used for temporary or permanent living quarters. It also defined a structure as something constructed or erected and requiring a location on the ground or attachment to something located there. During a public hearing in August 2024, the county planning commission recommended approving Rice's application with conditions. These included constructing a berm along the boundary adjoining residential properties and prohibiting waste incineration.The county commissioner considered the application at a public hearing on September 4, 2024. Norhaven representatives and other residents opposed the proposal, arguing that the 1,000-foot restriction would be violated. Nevertheless, the commissioner approved the permit with conditions, including a requirement to maintain the separation distance from residential homes.Developer challenged the permit approvalOn October 3, 2024, Norhaven filed a petition seeking judicial review of the county's decision. It maintained that the facility would violate the zoning ordinance because 46 planned townhomes were within the restricted distance. During a July 2025 hearing, Norhaven argued that residential dwellings did not need to be physically constructed to receive protection under the zoning provisions. Rice, however, maintained that the ordinance applied only to residential structures existing when the permit application was submitted.In September 2025, the trial court sent the matter back to the county commissioner for additional factual findings on whether the proposed waste handling area was within 1,000 feet of any residential dwelling. The commissioner subsequently found that the facility was at least 1,000 feet from every residential dwelling being used when Rice submitted his application. The finding relied on hearing testimony confirming that, although some site work had taken place, construction of the townhomes had not begun.On January 5, 2026, the trial court rejected Norhaven's remaining arguments and upheld the permit approval. The developer then appealed the decision.Appeals court upheld the conditional use permitNorhaven raised three main arguments before the Georgia Court of Appeals. It challenged the trial court's approach to reviewing the county proceedings, its decision to send the matter back for additional findings and its conclusion that the commissioner had followed the instructions on remand. The appeals court acknowledged that the trial court had incorrectly interpreted the scope of its review as being limited to the public hearing transcript. However, it found that this error did not affect the outcome because the trial court had also considered the relevant zoning provisions.On the central issue, the appeals court concluded that the definition of a residential dwelling required an actual constructed building or structure intended for living quarters. Undeveloped land planned for future residential construction did not qualify as a dwelling under the ordinance. The court also found sufficient evidence supporting the commissioner's conclusion that no residential dwellings had been constructed on Norhaven's property when Rice applied for the permit. It therefore rejected the developer's arguments and affirmed the trial court's decision.The November 2 ruling left Rice's conditional use permit in place. It did not determine whether the proposed townhomes could eventually be affected by the facility's operations. Instead, the decision established that the specific 1,000-foot restriction did not apply to homes that were still unbuilt when the permit application was submitted.You use AI every day. articles.title: Florida couple reconciled after wife received their home in first divorce settlement; years later, a second divorce turned the $430,000 property into a legal dispute
articles.summary: A Florida couple’s second divorce led to a dispute over a home worth about $430,000, years after they had reconciled and ended an earlier divorce case.
articles.body: A Florida couple’s second divorce led to a dispute over a home worth about $430,000, years after they had reconciled and ended an earlier divorce case. During the first proceedings, the couple signed a quitclaim deed transferring the home to the wife alone. A marital settlement agreement also described the home as her sole property. But the couple later reconciled, and their first divorce action was dismissed.When the husband filed for divorce again in 2023, the wife argued that the home should remain her nonmarital property. According to Florida’s Fourth District Court of Appeal, the property was correctly classified as a marital asset because the transfer occurred while the marriage remained intact.Florida couple bought home in 2011 with a $75,000 informal mortgageThe couple married in 1997 and bought the home in 2011 from Jacqueline Leavitt. The purchase involved an informal mortgage of $75,000, documented in a note signed by both spouses. It required 20 annual instalments of $5,400, including 4% interest, starting in April 2012. Both later told the court that no payments had been made.The couple’s first divorce case began in 2015. While it was pending, they signed a quitclaim deed transferring the property to the wife alone. They also signed a corrective deed to fix its legal description. In January 2017, they entered a marital settlement agreement stating that the home was the wife’s sole property. The first case was later dismissed after the couple reconciled.How did a couple's reconciliation lead to a second dispute over their homeThe settlement agreement said that, if the home was sold, the proceeds would first be used to pay mortgages. If money remained, the husband would receive $10,000, and the wife would receive the rest. After reconciling, the couple did not cancel the quitclaim deed.In the second divorce case, filed by the husband in 2023, he sought an equitable division of marital assets and liabilities. The wife asked for the home to be awarded to her, arguing that her husband had quitclaimed his interest in 2016. The appeal court said she had not preserved an argument that the agreement should determine the home’s status in court.Wife's earlier claim to $430,000 home failed in second divorceThe appeal court said the 2015 divorce petition could not set the date for classifying the property because that case had been dismissed without a final judgment. The parties were therefore treated as if the first action had never been brought. For the second divorce, the relevant date was the filing of the 2023 petition.The court said the husband transferred his interest during the marriage. It counted as either an asset acquired by the wife during the marriage or an interspousal gift. Both categories are marital assets under Florida law. The court upheld the judge’s decision to classify the home as marital property and upheld the decision to make the wife responsible for the Leavitt note.The court sent other parts of the divorce judgment back for reviewThe appeal court reversed other parts of the judgment. The spouses had agreed to keep debts in their own names, and the judge had said no debts would be divided. The written judgment nevertheless distributed credit card debts, so the court ordered those debts removed from the calculation, except for the Leavitt mortgage.It found conflicting figures for furnishings, as the judgment listed $2,000 for a bedroom set and $30,000 for remaining furnishings, but did not include the latter amount in its distribution calculation. The appeal court also removed $5,779.75 in child support arrears, which had not been raised at trial, and ordered the court to delete the arrears from its later judgment.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court records. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the property dispute or the financial arrangements between the couple. The information reflects the findings and ruling of the Florida Fourth District Court of Appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Julia Child bought a Cambridge home in the 1960s and donated it to a college in 2001; the house where she once filmed cooking shows has now sold for $6.525 million, while her old kitchen sits in a museum
articles.summary: Julia Child’s former home in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has found a new owner, selling for $6.525 million just weeks after hitting the market.
articles.body: Julia Child’s former home in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has found a new owner, selling for $6.525 million just weeks after hitting the market. The historic property, where the celebrated chef spent four decades and filmed several of her television cooking shows, has changed considerably since her time there. While the house has undergone a major renovation, the kitchen that became familiar to millions of viewers has been preserved at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History. Details of the sale were reported by Mansion Global, while property records and the Smithsonian provide further information about the house and its culinary history. The property, located at 103 Irving Street, was built in 1889 and covers approximately 6,321 square feet. It has six bedrooms spread across three floors and sits on a quarter-acre plot. Although its interiors have been updated over the years, the Victorian-style exterior retains much of its original character. The house also features hardwood floors, French doors and a contemporary kitchen, a considerable departure from the space that once became a familiar sight on American television.Child and her husband, Paul, moved into the Cambridge property in 1961 after spending several years living in Europe. The kitchen was designed around her needs, with Paul helping create a practical space where everything was within easy reach. The couple installed unusually high maple countertops to accommodate Julia's height and used pegboards to hang pots, pans and cooking utensils. Paul even outlined the shape of each item on the boards, making it easier to return everything to its place after use.The kitchen eventually became more than just a place where the chef prepared meals. It served as the setting for several of her television programmes, particularly those she filmed in the 1990s. These included In Julia's Kitchen with Master Chefs, Baking with Julia and Julia & Jacques Cooking at Home. Her earlier television success, The French Chef, had helped introduce generations of American viewers to French cooking through Boston's WGBH television station.When Child decided to leave Cambridge and return to California in 2001, she donated the house and her office to Smith College, where she had studied. The college subsequently sold the property. She also donated her kitchen and its contents to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, ensuring that the space where she had spent so much of her life would remain accessible to the public.Today, visitors to the Smithsonian can see the kitchen reconstructed with its original cabinets, maple countertops, appliances, utensils and signature pegboards. The museum documented the room before dismantling it, allowing the team to recreate its arrangement as closely as possible. The collection includes around 1,200 objects from Child's home, preserving not just the equipment she used but also the everyday details that made the kitchen distinctly hers.The property's latest sale has also brought renewed attention to its place in Cambridge's history. In August 2026, the Cambridge City Council voted in favour of installing a commemorative plaque at the house to recognise Child's connection to the neighbourhood. However, the wording still needs to be finalised, and the new owner's approval will be required before it can be installed.Child's former home now belongs to a new owner, but its association with the chef remains an important part of its story. While the kitchen where she once cooked for television audiences has found a permanent home in a museum, the Cambridge property continues to carry the history of the woman who helped make cooking more approachable for millions of people.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2018, construction workers cut trees and shrubs up to 150 feet beyond an Oregon property line; eight years later, an appeals court upheld $810,000 in treble damages against the neighbouring landowner
articles.summary: A construction project can become an expensive dispute when work crosses a property boundary.
articles.body: A construction project can become an expensive dispute when work crosses a property boundary. In Oregon, a landowner alleged that workers clearing an adjoining parcel removed trees, shrubs and other plants from as much as 150 feet inside his property. A jury found that the timber trespass was intentional and awarded him $810,000 in treble damages.In an opinion dated April 8, 2026, the Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment in Butori v. Bosma, case number A181266. The decision, available on Justia, rejected challenges to the evidence and to Henry Bosma's personal liability. The court found sufficient evidence that he personally directed or caused the clearing.Construction clearing crossed the property lineThe dispute involved adjoining properties known as Government Lots 6 and 7. Tom Butori owned Lot 6, while Bosma Enterprises Inc. (in which Bosma had an ownership interest) owned Lot 7. Butori alleged that Bosma hired VB Construction in 2018 to carry out work on the neighbouring property.During the work, trees, shrubs and other plants were removed from an area Butori said belonged to him, extending approximately 150 feet beyond the boundary. The defendants disputed where the property line lay and presented competing evidence. The jury found in Butori's favour and determined that the timber trespass was willful or intentional. Oregon law allows treble damages when someone willfully or intentionally cuts, injures or removes trees or shrubs from another person's land. The judgment awarded Butori $810,000.Earlier settlement helped establish knowledgeOn appeal, Bosma and Bosma Enterprises raised three challenges. They first argued that the trial court had improperly allowed Butori to testify about his understanding of the boundary after meeting the county surveyor.The appeals court noted that the trial judge had stopped Butori when he began repeating what the surveyor had told him. But his later testimony concerned his own belief about the boundary, based partly on his observations and the meeting. Because he did not repeat an out-of-court statement by the surveyor, the testimony was not hearsay. The defendants also challenged evidence of an earlier timber trespass settlement between the same parties involving the general area near the disputed boundary. They argued that it could lead jurors to assume they had admitted fault.The trial court admitted the agreement for a limited purpose: showing that Bosma knew the boundary was disputed, which could help jurors decide whether the later clearing was intentional or accidental. The judge removed the amount paid under the earlier settlement and instructed jurors not to treat the agreement as proof of liability. The appeals court found no error in that decision.Court found Bosma could be personally liableThe defendants' final argument was that there was insufficient evidence to hold Bosma personally responsible, rather than the company that owned the neighbouring property. The appeals court explained that a person is not automatically protected from liability for their own actions merely because they act through a business. The evidence had to allow the jury to find that Bosma personally directed or caused the clearing.A surveyor testified that Bosma had hired him in 2011 to prepare a topographical map for work near the property line. During an on-site discussion, the surveyor warned him to stay within the right of way, but described Bosma as dismissive of his understanding of the boundary. The surveyor also testified that Bosma hired him again in 2018 to document clearing that had already taken place. Based on an earlier survey, the witness located that clearing on Butori's property. The appeals court said the jury could reasonably infer that Bosma personally caused the clearing and acted intentionally.$810,000 award remains in placeThe Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment, leaving the $810,000 treble-damages award intact. The decision relied on the jury's finding that the trespass was willful or intentional and evidence that Bosma knew the boundary was disputed before the 2018 work. The ruling rejected all three challenges and preserved Butori's award.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
